## Goals of the course

- **Apply** bash scripting to execute bioinformatics software, and Python/R scripts

- **Apply** bash scripting to **execute** batch jobs on a high performance cluster.

- **Manage** software dependencies reproducibly using container-based technologies such as Docker/Apptainer containers or EasyBuild modules

- **Utilize** workflow managers to process multiple files in a multi-step Workflow Development Langauge (WDL) workflow.

## Running scripts from R or Python

Recall using `module load` to load in pre-installed software on the cluster:

```         
module load fhR
module load fhPython
```

. . .

For running a R script in the command line:

```         
Rscript rnorm.R
```

. . .

For running a Python script in the command line:

```         
python3 random_num.py
```

## Executable Programs

Bash scripts are "executable" programs, meaning they are independent programs that can run on their own without other software, such as `Rscript` or `python3`.

. . .

Other "executable" programs may include `bwa` for sequence alignment.

. . .

When we call an executable program, the system first looks into all the executable list of programs, defined by the variable `$PATH`. We can look at contents of `$PATH`, which shows all the folders it will consider to run an executable program.

. . .

```         
clo2@rhino03:~/bash_for_bio/scripts/week1$ echo $PATH
/app/bin:/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin:/usr/games:/usr/local/games:/snap/bin
```

. . .

The executable program `tell_the_time.sh` is located in the current directory, and not in `$PATH`. How do we run it?

. . .

```         
clo2@rhino03:~/bash_for_bio/scripts/week1$ tell_the_time.sh
tell_the_time.sh: command not found
```

. . .

Rather, we need to run with `./` (why? see this [post](https://unix.stackexchange.com/questions/4430/why-do-we-use-dot-slash-to-execute-a-file-in-linux-unix).)

```         
clo2@rhino03:~/bash_for_bio/scripts/week1$ ./tell_the_time.sh
-bash: ./tell_the_time.sh: Permission denied
```

## File permissions

`ls -l tell_the_time.sh`

What can you do with files?

| Type | Description | Abbreviation | Example |
|----|----|----|----|
| Read | Level can only read contents of file | `r` | Reading the contents of a text file |
| Write | Level can write to the file | `w` | Appending an entry to the end of a log |
| Execute | Level can run the file as an executable | `x` | Running the software `samtools` |

. . .

These types of actions have varying levels of permissions that can be set.

| Level       | Description           |
|-------------|-----------------------|
| Owner-level | The owner of the file |
| Group-level | The group of the file |
| Everyone    | The rest of the world |

## File permissions

```         
folder everyone_else
|      |     
-rw-rw----
 |  |
 you group
```

The 2nd to 4th letters define your own access to the files. The

```         
rw-
```

Means that you have **r**ead and **w**rite access. If we had the following:

```         
rwx
```

That would mean we have read, write, and e**x**ecute access.

[More info here](https://www.redhat.com/en/blog/linux-file-permissions-explained).

## Changing Permissions

Make the file executable:

`chmod +x tell_the_time.sh`

Then,

`./tell_the_time.sh`

## Writing your first bash script

Take a look at `sam_count_basic.sh`

```         
#!/bin/bash                           
module load SAMtools/1.19.2-GCC-13.2.0  
samtools view -c CALU1_combined_final.sam > CALU1_combined_final.sam.counts.txt
module purge
```

. . .

`#!/bin/bash` denotes how this script is going to be executed.

. . .

`>` denotes the output file content of the command `samtools view`

. . .

`module purge` "unloads" any loaded software.

. . .

Run the script:

`./sam_count_basic.sh`

## Repeating this script for many files

Suppose you have `sample1.sam`, `sample2.sam`, `sample3.sam`, etc. that you want to run `samtools view` on.

. . .

Can we give our script an input argument denoting what the input sample is? Such as:

`./sam_count_basic.sh sample1.sam`

## Variables in bash scripting

In Bash, we can declare a variable by using `<variable_name>=<value>`. (No spaces!!!)

. . .

```         
my_variable="ggplot2"

echo "My favorite R package is ${my_variable}"
```

. . .

Refer to variables using braces to be safe, ie:

```         
my_var="chr1"
echo "${my_var}_1.vcf.gz"
```

. . .

Example:

```         
#!/bin/bash                           
module load SAMtools/1.19.2-GCC-13.2.0  
input_file="CALU1_combined_final.sam"
samtools view -c ${input_file} > ${input_file}.counts.txt
module purge
```

## Input argument variables

In Bash scripting, there are special pre-defined variables `$1`, `$2`, etc. that refer to the input arguments of a bash script.

For instance,

```         
#!/bin/bash  
echo "My favorite R package is ${1}"
```

And you run the script with

```         
./script.sh bioconductor
```

You will get the output:

"My favorite R package is bioconductor".

## Putting it together

```         
#!/bin/bash                           
module load SAMtools/1.19.2-GCC-13.2.0  
samtools view -c ${1} > ${1}.counts.txt
module purge
```

```         
./sam_count.sh CALU1_combined_final.sam
```

## Challenging example

```         
#!/bin/bash
module load BWA/0.7.17-GCCcore-11.2.0
input_fastq=${1}
# strip path and suffix
base_file_name="${input_fastq%.fastq}"
base_file_name=${base_file_name##*/}
echo "running $input_fastq"
sample_name="SM:${base_file_name}"
read_group_id="ID:${base_file_name}"
platform_info="PL:Illumina"
ref_fasta_local="/shared/biodata/reference/iGenomes/Homo_sapiens/UCSC/hg19/Sequence/BWAIndex/genome.fa" 

bwa mem \
      -p -v 3 -M \
      -R "@RG\t${read_group_id}\t${sample_name}\t${platform_info}" \
      "${ref_fasta_local}" "${input_fastq}" > \
      "${base_file_name}.sam"
      
module purge
```

. . .

```         
./run_bwa.sh CALU1_combined_final.fastq
```

## Input arguments for R and Python scripts

Suppose that you want to run your bash script on a R script, which would require something like...

```         
#!/bin/bash
module load fhR
Rscript process_data.R ${1}
module purge
```

How do we deal with input arguments for the *R script* `process_data.R`?
